planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light with high humidity; the near-black spathe darkens further with cooler night temperatures and lower light, so give it a slightly dimmer spot than standard red Anthurium cultivars for the deepest color.

directions: Anthurium andraeanum 'Otazu' is a florist and collector cultivar prized for its glossy, deeply maroon-to-black heart-shaped spathe, one of the darkest colors bred in the andraeanum group, contrasted against a matching dark spadix. Pot in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix of bark, perlite, and peat, and keep evenly moist without letting the roots sit in water. Provide bright, filtered light — too little light produces smaller, less richly colored spathes, while direct sun scorches the foliage. Feed lightly during active growth to sustain repeat flowering through the year.
sources: International Aroid Society — Anthurium andraeanum cultivar notes
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Anthurium andraeanum culture

planting.note: Grow as a terrestrial or basket specimen in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix with high humidity; the large rosette of corrugated leaves needs room to spread and benefits from consistent warmth year-round.

directions: Anthurium villosum is a bird's-nest-type species from the Ecuadorian rainforest, forming a bold rosette of long, heavily corrugated, dark blackish-green leaves with a rough, textured surface that gives the species its name. It grows terrestrially or as a low epiphyte in deep shade beneath the forest canopy, so it tolerates lower light than many showier velvet anthuriums. Keep the chunky bark-based mix consistently moist but never waterlogged, and maintain high humidity to prevent leaf-edge browning. Its architectural, sculptural form makes it a favorite among serious aroid collectors rather than the mass houseplant market.
sources: International Aroid Society — Anthurium species descriptions
Exotic Rainforest — Anthurium villosum cultivation notes

planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light with elevated humidity; the thick, quilted velvet leaves are slow-growing and appreciate a chunky, well-aerated mix that dries slightly between waterings.

directions: Anthurium splendidum is a Central American velvet-leaf species related to A. clarinervium and A. crystallinum, grown for its thick, heart-shaped, deep olive-green leaves with a quilted, almost puckered surface texture and pale contrasting veins. It is slower and more compact than its better-known velvet relatives, forming a dense rosette well suited to smaller pots and terrarium-style setups. Provide bright, filtered light and a chunky, orchid-bark-based substrate that drains quickly, since the thick roots are prone to rot in dense, wet soil. High humidity keeps the heavily textured leaves from developing crispy edges.
sources: International Aroid Society — Anthurium species descriptions
Selby Botanical Gardens — Aroid collection notes

planting.note: Provide a moss pole or bark totem for the plant to climb; young shingling leaves press flat against the support, so mist regularly and keep the climbing surface consistently damp to encourage tight adherence.

directions: Anthurium peltigerum is a hemiepiphytic 'shingling' species that presses its overlapping, glossy heart-shaped juvenile leaves flat against tree bark as it climbs, a growth habit shared with a handful of prized shingling aroids. Mature, unattached leaves become larger and more elongated. Grow it on a moss pole or cork slab in bright indirect light with high humidity, keeping the climbing medium evenly moist so aerial roots can attach and absorb moisture. It is slow to establish but forms a dramatic, tightly shingled column once settled, making it a favorite among collectors of climbing aroids.
sources: International Aroid Society — Anthurium species descriptions
Exotic Rainforest — Shingling Anthurium species notes

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; deepest spathe color develops with consistent warmth and moderate humidity rather than intense light, so avoid direct sun that fades the dark pigment.

directions: Anthurium andraeanum 'Black Love' is a widely sold potted cultivar bred for its glossy, deep maroon-black spathes that appear near-black in low light and warm burgundy in brighter conditions, held above the same emerald, heart-shaped foliage typical of andraeanum hybrids. Grow in a peat-and-bark potting mix that holds moisture but drains freely, and water when the top inch of soil dries slightly. Provide bright, indirect light and humidity above 50% for continuous spathe production, and remove spent flowers at the base of the stem to encourage new blooms.
sources: Costa Farms — Anthurium 'Black Love' plant care guide
American Society for Horticultural Science — Anthurium andraeanum breeding overview

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; an old European ornamental selection grown for its finely dissected, fern-like green foliage rather than fruit production.

directions: Laciniata is one of the oldest recorded elder cultivars, prized since at least the 17th century for its deeply cut, almost fern-like or parsley-like green foliage that gives the whole shrub a soft, airy texture unlike the coarse leaves of wild elder. Creamy white flat-topped flower clusters appear in early summer followed by small black berries, though it is grown chiefly as a foliage and texture accent in mixed borders rather than for harvest. Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the most finely divided leaves, and prune hard in late winter to renew vigorous, well-cut foliage each season, since older wood tends to produce coarser leaves.

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, fertile soil in partial shade, which helps prevent the gold leaf margins from scorching in hot afternoon sun.

directions: Aureomarginata is a long-cultivated heirloom elder valued for its crisp green leaves edged in bright gold, giving a brighter, more finely detailed look than solid golden-leaved forms. Flat clusters of creamy white flowers appear in early summer, followed by small black berries, though the shrub is grown primarily for season-long foliage interest rather than fruit. Provide partial shade or morning sun with afternoon protection in hot climates to keep the gold margins from bleaching or scorching, and cut back older stems in late winter to encourage fresh, well-marked new growth.

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to protect the gold variegation from midday sun scorch.

directions: Madonna is a compact, brightly variegated elder cultivar with broad green leaves boldly edged in creamy gold, lighting up a shaded corner of the border more strongly than older gold-margined forms. Flat clusters of white, faintly fragrant flowers open in early summer and mature into small black berries, but the shrub is grown as a foliage specimen rather than for fruit. Site it in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun to prevent the variegated margins from browning, and prune out any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the variegation strong.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost or set out divisions in spring; this variety tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than the typical species and needs no coddling once rooted in.

directions: Native to the eastern and southeastern United States, this variety carries broader, more sparsely toothed leaves and slightly larger flowerheads than the typical species, on somewhat shorter and stockier stems. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes into a tidy clump rather than running aggressively, blooming from late summer into fall with the same golden-orange rays and dark chocolate-brown cones. Established plants tolerate heavier clay soils and brief dry spells better than many black-eyed susans, and the persistent seed heads feed goldfinches through winter if left uncut.
